turns.speaker: Janai Nelson
turns.text: Twenty-eight months ago, this Court made it pellucidly clear that  Section 2 is constitutional and that there need not be a race-neutral map that is presented as part of the illustrative maps. Many questions that are presented by my opponents on the other side have been asked and answered in Milligan. What is also clear is that Louisiana is emblematic of the ongoing need for Section 2. For example, we're talking about how close this may come to intent or results. If we look simply at the evidence here in Louisiana, we see that Louisiana had shifting justifications for its map. Whenever it was presented with a map that met or beat its criteria and gave Black voters an equal opportunity to participate in the process, it rejected those maps. The court in Robinson also relied on the fact that there has never been a Black candidate elected on a statewide basis. Even  when white Democrats won an election in 2019, Black Democrats lost. My opponents here would  like to make this a partisan issue because they believe the case law will enable their case to prevail. But it does not. This is abo ut race. Section 2 in the Voting Rights Act is laser-focused on eliminating racial discrimination from our electoral process regardless of party. And if we look at many of the Black Congress people who were elected, they came out of Section 2 opportunity districts. They don't have to be majority-minority districts. Many of them are crossover districts. And so, if we remove Section 2, we also recognize that there will likely be a resurgence of discrimination because Section 2 plays a deterrent effect. States are drawing maps with Section 2 in mind. In fact, Local Rule 21 in Louisiana says that the State must comply with Section 2. The fact that HB1, which was the original map, was pre-cleared by the Department of Justice means very little. Retrogression is an entirely  different standard from what Section 2 is looking at. Retrogression means the State of Louisiana cannot go backwards. Section 2 is talking about whether there is active discrimin ation right now preventing the additional  opportunities for Black voters who meet all of the Gingles preconditions to have an equal opportunity to participate in the process. Requiring plaintiffs to control for party is helpful if that evidence exists, and it did to some extent in Robinson, where we put on evidence about Democratic elections and the preferences of white voters that still preferred white Democrats over Black Democrats. But that is not the only question. If that evidence is available, and I will remind the Court it's not often available if there aren't primary elections or if we are looking at more down-ballot elections, not just the congressional elections at issue here, that evidence is useful, but if there is significant racially polarized voting, that has already been shown to be probative of intentional  --of discrimination that comes very close to intentional discrimination. What Congress did in Section 2 was strike a very careful balance of using factors like White v. Regester, like the Zimmer  factors, to bring us as close to a finding of intent without making the full accusation and  without requiring that conclusion on the part of courts. So we should not downplay, as my opponents have, the robust nature and exacting requirements of a Gingles test and also remind ourselves that the City of Rome in 1980 made very clear that Congress can address effects beyond what the Fifteenth Amendment requires. I'll close by saying that in Bush v. Vera, this Court said that it must be particularly concerned about changing its decisions or rejecting stare decisis in cases that involve a sensitive political context like the one  --like this one. That calls the Court's legitimacy into question in a new unique way. My opponents here have not done the labor of showing that precedents should be overturned. They haven't addressed Janus. They haven't addressed Ramos. They've simply said that we should overturn or tweak the precedent that governs Section 2. And I would say that there's no record to support that in this case,  and this Court would be remiss to not require that if it is entertaining any significant modifications of Section 2. Any further neutering of Section 2 would resurrect the Fifteenth Amendment as a mere parchment promise, and we ask the Court to remand. Thank you.

turns.speaker: D. John Sauer
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  Respondents here seek judicial review of the Secretary's decisions to terminate Temporary Protected Status for Syria and Haiti. Yet Section 1254a(b)(5)(A) provides that there is no judicial review of any determination of  the Secretary with respect to the designation or termination or extension of a designation of a foreign state for Temporary Protected Status. That provision means what it says. "Determination" is hardly a rarely used word that broadly includes the Secretary's decisions, conclusions, or opinions. Both "any" and "with respect to" have an expansive  meaning and a broadening effect. The provision thus bars judicial review of both the Secretary's ultimate decision whether to designate, extend, or terminate and of each antecedent step along the way to that determination. Respondents' attempts to carve out  exceptions to the review bar would eviscerate it because virtually any substantive challenge could be recast as a procedural claim, as their own claims demonstrate. Moreover, their claims plainly cannot be raised without referring to or relying on the termination decisions, and they challenge the very kind of foreign-policy-laden judgments that are traditionally entrusted to the political branches. Even if their claims are not barred, they are meritless. The statute does not micromanage the degree of consultation with other agencies. Paragraph (b)(3) requires the Secretary to consider the national interest in  reviewing designations made under (b)(1)(C) because it requires her to determine whether the foreign state continues to meet the conditions for designation under paragraph (1). Far from demonstrating pretext, the fact that the Secretary exercised her discretion consistently is a virtue, not a vice. And the Miot Respondents' constitutional  claim is meritless under any standard of review. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  Congress struck a balance in the TPS statute. turns.speaker: Geoffrey M. Pipoly
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  For decades, administrations of both parties successfully terminated TPS designations without inviting litigation. They  did so by following the process Congress set forth in the TPS statute. The termination of Haiti's TPS was different. It was not the result of the mandatory review process but was instead a preordained result driven by the President's resolve to end TPS for Haiti no matter what. The reasons Secretary Noem gave for the termination were pretextual. The DHS documents that we already lodged with this Court show that the Secretary's purported review was a sham. Agency staff was "forced" to include rationales for termination that had no empirical support. The true reason for the termination of the  --for the termination is the President's racial animus towards non-white immigrants and bare dislike of Haitians in particular. The  President has disparaged Haitian TPS holders specifically as undesirables from a "shithole country," and days after falsely accusing them of "eating the dogs and eating the cats of Americans," he vowed that he would terminate  Haiti's TPS, and that is exactly what happened. Recognizing all this, the district court correctly postponed the termination. This Court should affirm. And I welcome the Court's questions.

It gets even more striking when you read the Haiti Respondents' brief, where, in the 11 pages or so in which they discuss the -- the merits of their claims, by the second or third page, they've kind of abandoned any pretense that what they're raising is procedural, and they're raising the whole panoply of substantive challenge -- APA -type challenges to this particular decision.

So, to the extent there is a  -- you know, a  -- a -- a -- a judicial -- or any exception to the judicial review bar here, their own briefs, I think, demonstrate that  it's going to collapse under its own weight.
There's been reference to the presidential directives that we're supposed to provide.
There is a presidential directive that was provided.
It was provided in the executive order.
And the President directed  the Secretary to ensure that TPS designations are "appropriately limited in scope" and only as long as necessary to achieve the -- the textual directives in the statute.

And that is what the  -- that is what the Secretary did here. And then, Justice Gorsuch, as to your question, I do think it's helpful to end this case by look  -- or end this argument by looking at their prayer for relief in their complaints, which says we are challenging the termination decision as to these two  --these two countries.
We are saying that that termination  decision was unlawful.
It should be declared unlawful.
It should be set aside under the  APA.
It should be postponed under Section 705.
And I think, at that point, at a very high level, we are looking at a  --a request for judicial review of the termination determination, and that is exactly what the statute bars.
Thank you.

turns.speaker: D. John Sauer
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  On April 2, President Trump determined that our exploding trade deficits had brought us to the brink of an economic and national security catastrophe.  He further pronounced  that the traffic of fentanyl and other opioids into our country has created a public health crisis, taking hundreds of thousands of American lives.  President Trump has declared that these emergencies are country-killing and not sustainable, that they threaten the bedrock of our national and economic security, and that fixing them will make America strong,  financially viable, and a respected country again.  Due to IEEPA tariffs, President Trump has negotiated agreements worth trillions of  dollars with major trading partners, including most recently China.  Unwinding those agreements, he warns, would expose us to ruthless trade retaliation by far more aggressive countries and drive America from strength to failure, with ruinous economic and  national security consequences.  In Dames & Moore against Regan, this Court held that IEEPA's sweeping and  unqualified language grants the President's actions the strongest presumption of validity and the widest latitude of judicial interpretation.  Yet plaintiffs argue that  tariffs, IEEPA's least blunt and most nimble tool, are virtually the only tool that Congress did not grant the President to deal with foreign emergencies.  That is wrong.  The phrase "regulate importation" plainly embraces tariffs, which  are among the most traditional and direct methods of regulating importation.  And plaintiffs concede that IEEPA authorizes quotas and other tariff equivalents.  The major questions doctrine does not apply here.  IEEPA confers major powers to  address major problems on the President, who is perhaps the most major actor in the realm of foreign affairs.  And the nondelegation doctrine casts no doubt on IEEPA because  Congress may assign the President broad authority regarding the conduct of foreign affairs, where he enjoys his own inherent Article II powers.  I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  Tariffs are taxes.  They take dollars from Americans' pockets and deposit them in the U.S.  Treasury.  Our founders gave that taxing power to Congress alone.  Yet, here, the  President bypassed Congress and imposed one of the largest tax increases in our lifetimes.  Many doctrines explain why this is illegal, like the presumption that Congress speaks clearly when it imposes taxes and duties and the major questions doctrine.  But it comes down to common sense. It's simply implausible that in enacting IEEPA Congress handed the President the power to  overhaul the entire tariff system and the American economy in the process, allowing him to set and reset tariffs on any and every product from any and every country at any and all times.  And, as Justices Gorsuch and Barrett just said, this is a one-way ratchet.  We will never get this power back if the government wins this case.  What president wouldn't veto  legislation to rein this power in and pull out the tariff power?  IEEPA is a sanction statute.  It's not a tax statute where Congress gave away the store.  Congress knows exactly how to delegate its tariff powers.  Every time for 238 years,  it's done so explicitly, always with real limits.  IEEPA looks nothing like those laws. It uses "regulate," which Congress has used hundreds of times, never once to include tariffs.  And it lacks the limits of every other tariff statute.  And that is why, even  though presidents have used IEEPA to impose economic sanctions thousands of times, no president in IEEPA's 50-year lifetime has ever tried to impose tariffs.  And the President bypassed statutes that do address tariffs, like Section 122 for large and serious trade deficits, but that imposes a clear guardrail, 15 percent cap,  150-day limit. This is Youngstown at its lowest ebb. If the government wins, another president could declare a climate emergency and impose huge tariffs without fines or  --without floors or ceilings, as Justice Gorsuch said.  My friend's answer?  This administration would declare it a hoax.  The next president may not quite say that.  This is an open -ended power to junk the tariff laws and is certainly not conveyed by the  -- by the word "regulate." I welcome the Court's questions.

If it never raises a dime of  revenue, these are the most effective use of these -- of this particular policy.  And I said there's two buckets there. One is, first of all, when it comes to the  trade deficit emergency, if no one ever pays the tariff, but, instead, they direct their consumption domestically and spur the creation or the rebuilding of our -- of our hollowed-out manufacturing base, that directly addresses the crisis.  It's more effective if no one ever pays the tariff.  That's the point of it, really.  You know, that's a fundamental point  of it.  And that's one piece of these.  And then, as to both of them, as to both of the declared emergencies, the tariffs are an incentive, a pressure point, leverage, bargaining chip, as the Court said in Dames Moore, to get countries to change their behavior to address the foreign-arising emergencies.  So, if you look, for example, to take a historical example, last week's trade deal with China, it unlocked access to rare earth minerals, which, of course, have a  critical national security aspect to them, and it got China for the very first time to change its policy with respect to fentanyl precursors, which is a crucial piece of that.  That -- those tariffs, if no one ever collects them, but the threat of imposing those  tariffs gets China and our other trading partners across the world to change their  behaviors in a way that addresses this, then that's the most effective use of the policy. So they're clearly regulatory tariffs, not taxes.  They are not  --they're not an exercise of the power to tax.  They are the exercise of the power to regulate foreign commerce.  And that's why the statute says "regulate."  It doesn't say "tax."  It says "regulate."  And -- and for that reason, we are squarely within the tradition that I was  talking about before of very broad, historically very broad, delegations of the power to regulate foreign commerce to the  President because he has inherent Article II authority in the area of  -- of -- of -- of foreign affairs, although not that.  It has to be delegated to him.  Otherwise, the delegate  -- delegation would be superfluous. And for all those reasons, we ask the Court to reverse both the decisions below.

turns.speaker: Jeffrey B. Wall
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  The FCC imposed more than $100 million of civil penalties on AT&T and Verizon, and the companies had no way to demand a jury trial. That's a straightforward violation of the Seventh Amendment and this Court's decision in Jarkesy. The government's only answer is that the penalties weren't binding. They were just  invitations to pay $100 million if you want. And that's wrong for at least four reasons. First, the statute says that the FCC issues a charging document, considers the party's response, and then assesses and imposes penalties. That's not voluntary language. Second, it's the same language Congress has used in many statutes, including the SEC statute in Jarkesy, and the government has never claimed it is voluntary. Third, there's an alternative procedure by which the Commission itself or an ALJ can assess and impose penalties, the same statutory language. The government appears to  accept that type of forfeiture order is binding. And, fourth, it's not how the FCC has read the statute for decades. Its regulation and guidance treat forfeiture orders as binding. These orders are Exhibit A. In bold, capital letters, they command payment by a particular date. If the government were right about the statute, it would just walk them into a constitutional problem. They want these forfeiture orders because they know that  legitimate parties pay 100 percent of the time. If your main regulator says that you are violating the law, you can't let that hang over your head indefinitely. But, to guarantee any judicial review, AT&T and Verizon have to give up the right to a  jury trial. It is hard to imagine a clearer case of penalizing the exercise of a fundamental constitutional right. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Michael Zuckerman
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  Decades ago, New Jersey exercised its autonomy to provide what it saw as an essential public good, a statewide public transportation system. This case asks whether that system is most like a private business, locality, or state agency. NJ Transit's features answer that question decisively. The state gave NJ Transit rulemaking authority subject to our APA. The state gave it law enforcement power for all criminal laws anywhere in New Jersey. The state authorized it to exercise eminent domain anywhere in New Jersey. The state gave the governor a veto over any proposed board action. And the governor appoints all board members, most with advice and consent, and has for-cause or at-will removal power over each. On top of that, New Jersey owns NJ Transit. NJ Transit has no property rights  against the state. And the state sharply limited NJ Transit's ability to raise revenue, cut costs, or issue debt, effectively promising to cover its annual deficits, as it always has. To be sure, as this Court wrote of the University of Arkansas some 70 years ago, our legislature called NJ Transit a body co rporate and politic. But just as that can't change the answer under precedent, my friends have identified no basis to abandon precedent. Instead, their lead alternative misconstrues original meaning and would convert this Court's inquiry into a game no state knew it was playing. That would render countless agencies, including core cabinet agencies, suable without consent overnight, even though this Court has never suggested that states experiment with efficiency at peril to their sovereignty. And my friends never even cite the stare decisis factors, overlooking the disruption their overhaul would yield. In short, NJ Transit looks nothing like a city or town and little like a private company. It looks a lot like a New Jersey state agency. That means plaintiffs must sue it  where the state has consented, in New Jersey. I welcome this Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Michael B. Kimberly
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  When a state establishes a new public entity, it has a choice. First, it can establish a traditional department, agency,  commission, bureau that is an entity of the government itself that uses state employees and state property to perform its functions and relies on the public fisc for its finances. Alternatively, it can establish a  public corporation. A public corporation is a state-created entity that bears two key features. First, it has a separate legal identity, and it's thus capable of suing and being sued in court in its own name, in its own discretion. Second, it holds its own assets and liabilities, meaning that it's responsible for paying debts, including adverse judgments, from its own resources. It is entirely the point of creating a public corporation that it is a distinct legal person, separate and apart from the state that creates it. And the reason is that it makes debt financing substantially easier because separate legal entities are not bound by the constitutional limitations on public debt. That's so under New Jersey's debt limitation clause. It's true also, we know, from Briscoe and Wister under the federal Bill of Credit Clause. It's also relatively easier to  administer a public corporation's resources, like its human resources, free from the bureaucracy and complications of state government. But, by creating a separate legal entity in this way and achieving these benefits, the state accepts a cost, and the cost is  --it follows from the creation of a separate legal entity, a separate legal person, and that's that it does not share in the state's sovereign immunity. That has been the consistent holding of this  Court for the last 200 years, since Planters' Bank in 1824 through the Kentucky Bank cases of the 1830s, Lincoln County in 1890, and Hopkins in 1911. blocks.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  When a state establishes a new public entity, it has a choice.

First, it can establish a traditional department, agency,  commission, bureau that is an entity of the government itself that uses state employees and state property to perform its functions and relies on the public fisc for its finances. Alternatively, it can establish a  public corporation.
A public corporation is a state-created entity that bears two key features.
First, it has a separate legal identity, and it's thus capable of suing and being sued in court in its own name, in its own discretion.
Second, it holds its own assets and liabilities, meaning that it's responsible for paying debts, including adverse judgments, from its own resources.
It is entirely the point of creating a public corporation that it is a distinct legal person, separate and apart from the state that creates it.

And the reason is that it makes debt financing substantially easier because separate legal entities are not bound by the constitutional limitations on public debt. That's so under New Jersey's debt limitation clause.
It's true also, we know, from Briscoe and Wister under the federal Bill of Credit Clause.
It's also relatively easier to  administer a public corporation's resources, like its human resources, free from the bureaucracy and complications of state government.

But, by creating a separate legal entity in this way and achieving these benefits, the state accepts a cost, and the cost is  --it follows from the creation of a separate legal entity, a separate legal person, and that's that it does not share in the state's sovereign immunity.
That has been the consistent holding of this  Court for the last 200 years, since Planters' Bank in 1824 through the Kentucky Bank cases of the 1830s, Lincoln County in 1890, and Hopkins in 1911.
Our position is consistent with those cases and with more recent cases like Hess and Lewis.
New Jersey Transit's position is not.
And I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Kannon K. Shanmugam
turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  This case involves an unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct.  Boulder is suing Petitioners under  Colorado law on the theory that their global conduct increased the global use of fossil  fuels, which led to an increase in global greenhouse-gas emissions, which contributed to global climate change, which resulted in global harms.  Our constitutional system does not permit state law to be used in that manner. The Constitution bars the application of state law to certain inherently federal areas.  When the states entered the Union, the plan of the Convention required them to surrender certain preexisting powers in order to ensure each state's equal sovereignty.  Because of the ambient nature of air and water and the conflicting rights of states, this Court has held for over a century that  federal law governs interstate pollution claims.  That principle applies with even  greater force to claims involving global climate change.  In addition, the Constitution's prohibition on extraterritorial regulation  precludes a state from extending its law beyond its borders to regulate global conduct with  global effects.  A state does not have the power to regulate out-of-state conduct based solely on attenuated effects on the state.  What is more, the use of state law to regulate global climate change would substantially interfere with the nation's  foreign policy.  And far from authorizing the application of state law, the Clean Air Act  independently preempts any effort by one state to impose its law on emissions originating in others. If Boulder's claims are allowed to go forward, some 90,000 municipalities across the country will have the ability to make national  and international energy policy by asking juries to impose catastrophic damages on selected fossil -fuel producers. Put simply, that is not the constitutional scheme that the Founders adopted.  The Colorado Supreme Court's judgment  should accordingly be reversed.  I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Kannon K. Shanmugam
turns.text: Sure, Justice Thomas. Our view is that the Court has both statutory and constitutional jurisdiction.  I'll address those in turn.  On statutory jurisdiction, our view is that Atlantic Richfield is directly on point. It could not be clearer as a matter of Colorado law that the proceeding below was a self-contained original proceeding, which gives rise to jurisdiction in this Court under Section 1257. Boulder's argument to the contrary is that because this case did not involve a formal writ proceeding directed at the lower court, that it falls outside the scope of Atlantic Richfield.  But, in Atlantic Richfield itself, this Court attached no weight to the form of the underlying proceeding.  Instead, the Court  relied on the fact that it was a self-contained proceeding.  In fact, this proceeding contained many of the hallmarks of a writ proceeding. The Colorado Supreme Court ordered the trial court to respond to its order to show cause and then discharged the order to show cause at the end of the proceeding.  And the Colorado Supreme Court's move away from formal writs is not unusual.  As the brief of the state  -- former state supreme court justices points out, many states have  made that move toward a more informal label for their proceedings.  The key point is that in Colorado, as elsewhere, these original proceedings are distinct from ordinary appellate proceedings, even interlocutory appellate proceedings.  In Colorado, there are separate rules, Rule 21 and Rule 4.2, that govern each.  As to constitutional jurisdiction, I think our submission here is a straightforward one.  Because this case is coming from a state  court, you look to the injuries suffered by the Petitioners, who were the defendants in the lower court proceeding.  The decision below  definitively adjudicated our legal rights, and it did so in a way that was binding not just in this case but in other cases in Colorado as well.  So not only are my clients exposed to a greater risk of liability as a result of the fact that one of our central defenses has been knocked out, but, in a very real sense, we have lost the right to be free from state regulation, which was how this Court characterized the loss of a preemption defense  in NCAA versus Murphy, and as a result, we will suffer an injury.  So that personal stake, in  our view, is sufficient for Article III purposes.

turns.speaker: Kevin K. Russell
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  Since the Founding, states have had the power to provide tort remedies for injuries  occurring within their borders even when the conduct causing those injuries occurred elsewhere.  When somebody in New York defames a citizen of Boulder on national television or  somebody in California releases a computer virus on the Internet or a biological virus into the world and it causes mass damage in Colorado, it has never been thought that only federal law can provide a remedy simply because  the tortious conduct and the injury occurred in different states, because the harm was widespread, the damages were large, or the defendants were part of an important industry.  And applying state law to such cases has never been viewed as one state impermissibly projecting its law nationwide.  To be sure, specific constitutional provisions limit choice of law and place other constraints  on the extraterritorial effects of state law.  But Petitioners invoke none of those provisions here.  Instead, they invite this  Court to find in the structure of the Constitution a judicial power to declare some subject matters inherently federal and,  therefore, preempted not by Congressional enactments but by Congressional silence.  That claim inverts the constitutional structure and risks preemption being driven by judicial policy intuitions rather than anything  in the Constitution itself.  The structure of the Constitution places residual authority to preempt state laws  with undesirable nationwide effects in Congress, not the courts.  Accordingly, in AEP, this Court held that preemption of global  warming nuisance claims is governed by the preemptive force of the Clean Air Act, citing Ouellette, which applied ordinary statutory preemption principles and concluded that state law could apply. Here, the statute does not preempt Respondents' deception and other claims against non-emitters not subject to the Act. But all of this must await another case because Petitioners have failed to establish this Court's jurisdiction to hear this interlocutory appeal.  I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Kannon K. Shanmugam
turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice.  Just three points on rebuttal.  First, the breadth of Boulder's theory here is astonishing.  First, there is no limit under Boulder's theory on who could be sued. My friend, Mr. Russell, cites personal  jurisdiction and the Dormant Commerce Clause.  But, under Boulder's theory, Boulder could tag me with personal jurisdiction when I am in Colorado in two weeks and sue me on a  nuisance claim for refilling my car and thereby contributing to global climate change.  There  is simply no limit, and personal jurisdiction provides cold comfort in that regard.  Similarly, there's no limit on who can sue.  We haven't heard anything this morning to suggest that the band of potential plaintiffs would be limited to the mere 90,000 municipalities across the country.  Any individual who has suffered the effects of  climate change could sue under Boulder's theory as well.  Second, the shortest line to a -- an appropriately cabined and narrowed decision  here is to rely on the equal sovereignty principle.  In particular, the Court can rely on this Court's case law from Missouri versus Illinois right through to AEP in this particular context.  We do believe that the conceptual framework for that is set out in Franchise Tax Board versus Hyatt, in which the Court said that there are certain areas involving  conflicting rights where states cannot apply the applicable rule of decision.  And the Court can certainly say, for the reasons given by my friend, Ms. Harris, that that reasoning is reinforced by the extraterritoriality principle because there is  simply no precedent for extending any state's authority as far as Boulder is suggesting.  My friend, Mr. Russell, cites none. And third and finally, especially given the foreign affairs implications -- and remember that 90 percent of greenhouse-gas emissions occur outside the United States -- this is a matter for the political branches on the federal level in the first instance.  As the brief set out in some length, in this area, the President and Congress have struck a careful balance between energy production on the one hand and greenhouse-gas reductions on the other.  Congress can always act to authorize these claims if it so chooses.  But administrations of both political parties have opposed liability schemes on the international level.  There's no warrant for  countenancing one on the domestic level.  In conclusion, this case and others like it reflect an all -too -regrettable trend of trying to resolve major political issues in court rather than leaving them to the political branches where they belong.  Climate change is  certainly one of the most pressing issues of the day, but we would submit that this is  exactly the wrong way to go about resolving it. And so we would submit that the judgment of the Colorado Supreme Court should be reversed.  Thank you.

turns.speaker: Sopan Joshi
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  A permit application is not final agency action.  It's a request to someone else to take action.  Filing a permit application triggers a back -and-forth process whose outcome is, by definition, a moving target until a decision on the permit is issued.  Treating an  application as final would just lead to a multiplicity of suits throughout a permitting  process, which I think defeats the whole point of the finality requirement.  Now Respondent says that the application reflects some internal Air Force  decision to continue these activities for the next three years if Guam issues a permit.  But the "if" is precisely the kind of contingency that makes this not final.  Respondent also points out that the application enabled the old permit's expiration date to be tolled or extended.  But that is, at most, an incidental or indirect effect of the application, really, of Guam EPA's failure to rule on the application.  The direct and appreciable legal consequences of that extension flow from the terms of the old  permit, which Respondent has not challenged.  Now Respondent's claim also fails on the merits.  RCRA is a comprehensive statute specifically targeting hazardous waste and specifically specifying which environmental  review must occur at each step of a reticulated permit process.  Respondent's attempt to take all of NEPA and just shove it into the application stage is not only duplicative of RCRA's requirements, which are the functional equivalent, but inconsistent with RCRA's specification of when each of those requirements should occur through the permitting process.  All of that said, I don't think you need to actually address the interaction of NEPA and RCRA in this case because NEPA, by its terms, does not apply to non-final agency actions.  And so, if you agree with us, as I  think you should, that the application is not final agency action, that would not only  resolve the threshold issue in the case; it would also have the effect of resolving Respondent's claim on the merits here.  I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Caroline A. Flynn
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  The Air Force was required to comply with NEPA before choosing to continue open detonation on Tarague Beach.  And we can obtain  judicial review of that violation now.  On the question whether NEPA applies, the government's position is simply atextual. Congress has told us that NEPA is displaced only when it is excluded pursuant to another provision of law or there is a clear and fundamental conflict between NEPA and another law's requirements.  That aligns with this Court's precedent, the strong presumption against  implied repeals, and Congress's longstanding practice of drafting express exclusions to NEPA when it wants them.  The government's response is that RCRA is specifically about hazardous waste.  But,  because the laws can be harmonized, that observation can't carry the day.  Indeed, NEPA is meant to be harmonized with other environmental laws in this way.  It is what  agencies call an umbrella law.  It is meant to consolidate and streamline all required  environmental analysis at an early juncture to ensure a better decision and better planning.  So, if the Air Force was wrong to ignore NEPA here, the only question should be when Prutehi Guahan can get judicial review of that violation.  The Air Force's decision to  continue OD at this location and submitting the renewal application was not tentative, and its  application implementing the decision had, among other things, the concrete effect of  authorizing open detonation operations past the date when they otherwise would have ended.  The government is instead pushing a rule where the fact that the Air Force's  decision required external sign-off means that it can't be final as a matter of law, perhaps, apparently, not even after that external sign-off occurs.  That does not align with this Court's pragmatic approach to finality, and it is especially senseless when it comes to our claim of a procedural violation here.  Indeed, this Court has already said in Ohio Forestry Association versus Sierra Club that a litigant with standing can "complain of a NEPA failure at the time it takes place for the claim can never get riper."  There is  nothing to be gained here by delaying our challenge to the Air Force's own decision-making about its own operations until a non-federal agency has made a different determination under a different law.  I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice.  Just a few points.  First, to address the questions that Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kavanaugh had, our  position, just to be clear, is that the claim, as we understand it, and I think Ms. Flynn confirmed, was that they are saying the  submission of the RCRA application is final agency action.  We don't think that's final agency action.  And, indeed, the submission of the application, our position is, that that is just not agency action at all.  It'll never become final.  It's just an application.  The final permit, when it issues, will be final, but it'll be final from the regulating entity, Guam EPA, or federal EPA if it's Iowa.  As far as when the Air Force's action becomes final, I mean, if it's a case where, as Justice Thomas was suggesting, if after receiving a permit the agency issued an order saying, now go blow up these waste munitions on Guam, that would be an order.  That would be a  final agency action.  If Respondent wants to bring a claim saying, even absent such an order, there is a silent, implicit order, we can have that fight. We'd probably oppose that.  I'm sure they would say, no, there really is an order, and that would be a final agency action.  But that would have nothing to do with the RCRA permit.  It would have nothing to do with the RCRA permit application, which is what we're concerned with here.  And that gets me to my second point, which is Ms. Flynn said she wasn't worried about opening the floodgates.  I don't see how.  If you find that submission of a RCRA permit application is final agency action because the applicant happens to be a federal  agency, I don't know how you distinguish it from any one of the tens of thousands of permit applications that federal agencies file and hold at the current time.  Every single application would be final action, which could immediately trigger a lawsuit.  And it doesn't have to be a procedural lawsuit, as Ms. Flynn said.  It  could be anything.  It could be your application was arbitrary and capricious  because you didn't consider X, Y, and Z.  You shouldn't have applied for it.  You should have decided to do something different.  And if the application is revised, you're going to have another lawsuit, three years of litigation in between.  And then, when the final permit issues, I suppose we'll have yet another one.  So I think the floodgates are real. And, yes, Ms. Flynn is right that once there is some final action, a permit is issued, if the agency issues an order and does something, there will be a lawsuit then. That's unavoidable in our system. But the whole point of the finality rule is to challenge all of the challenges into a single proceeding at the end.  Finally, I just want to say, in terms of, Justice Alito, you were asking about conflict and impossibility and when do both statutes apply, I don't think it's right that there has to be a metaphysical impossibility of complying with both statutes.  I think a  conflict can be just inconsistency between the two, with a specific and a general.  And, again, the best case for that I think I'd cite is an environmental case. It's Home Builders, which we cite in our brief. And that was one where the Clean Water Act had, I think, nine criteria that EPA had to look at and see if they were satisfied, and the claim that the plaintiffs brought there was:  Well, by its terms, the Endangered Species Act could also apply to this situation.  And the Court said we are not going to engraft additional requirements.  Given how  reticulated the Clean Water Act is with nine requirements, we're not going to engraft a tenth.  I think the same would be true here. Unless the Court has further questions, we'd ask to reverse.

turns.speaker: Jeffrey W. Chen
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  Section 511(a) reaches questions necessary to a decision under a law that affects the provision of benefits.  Text,  context, structure, and the government's own longstanding practice make clear that 511(a) does not reach constitutional challenges to statutes.  Start with the text.  A decision under a statute is a decision in accordance with the statute.  It applies the statute as written. That's how this Court construed the same phrase in Robison.  And deciding a statute's validity  is not necessary to a decision under the statute.  The VA did not need to resolve  Section 5313's validity to reduce Mr. Johnson's benefits in accordance with Section 5313. Indeed, a decision to disregard Section 5313 as unconstitutional would obviously not be in accordance with Section 5313.  Context reinforces the point.  The Board of Veterans Appeals must make the VA's final decisions on all 511(a) matters, and no  one in 1988 would have understood deciding the constitutionality of statutes as necessary to  the BVA's decisions.  The BVA had long disclaimed authority to decide those questions, and the settled understanding was that administrative tribunals couldn't decide them.  If Congress meant to depart from those settled views, it would have done so clearly, but it didn't.  In fact, the government itself has long understood 511(a) exactly the way we do.  The VA responded to 511(a) by prohibiting the BVA from deciding challenges to statutes.  And the BVA has continued to disclaim authority over those questions.  The government's new reading would spurn decades of BVA practice and raise a host of anomalies and thorny questions.  Among other  things, it would empower the inferior officers of the BVA to render final decisions for the executive on whether to disregard acts of Congress.  That presents serious Article II concerns.  And none of the government's  proposed workarounds is consistent with the VJRA.  I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Kevin Joel Page
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  For two reasons, the courts below erred in deferring to the commentary when interpreting Guideline 2K2.1.  First, the proper rule for deference to guideline commentary is no deference. Nothing in the text of the Sentencing Reform Act suggests that courts must ever defer to commentary when interpreting a guideline, let alone defer on the  -- according to the extreme rule of Stinson.  That alone should resolve the question presented given the baseline expectation that courts independently determine the meaning of legal provisions.  That expectation dates back  to Marbury, and it should be especially hard to displace in the criminal setting, where respect for liberty demands that we turn square corners.  In fact, the Sentencing Reform Act is affirmatively incompatible with any deference regime.  Section -- Section 3553(a)(4) requires that the Commission set forth the range of imprisonment in the guidelines, not elsewhere. And Sections 994 and 995 of Title 28 attach detailed procedural requirements to the  amendment of guidelines, which requirements do not apply to guideline commentary.  Why would Congress bother to require detailed notice, public comment, 180 days of congressional review, and the approval of four  voting commissioners every time the -- the Commission amends a guideline if the Commission  could simply bind the courts to a new interpretation of the guideline without going through all of this simply by amending the commentary?  The second reason the courts below erred in affording Stinson deference is that if the Sentencing Reform Act leaves room for deference, the proper predicate is genuine ambiguity of the kind that survives every tool of construction, not the mere absence of plain or flat inconsistency, as Stinson suggests.  The rule applied below, which requires courts to construe guidelines in ways that they  think are wrong, certainly can't be found in the SRA's text, and it is not consistent with the judicial role.  I am pleased to take the Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Eric J. Feigin
turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  Our position is really the only one that's faithful to this Court's precedents. Stinson interpreted the Sentencing Reform Act to incorporate the same measure of deference for guidelines commentary that Seminole Rock gives to an agency's interpretation of its own rules.  Kisor then clarified what Seminole Rock deference means.  Add those two decisions  together and you get that Kisor applies to guidelines commentary. That said, I don't want to overstate the difference between our position and the position of the amicus here.  I  --we believe that even under Kisor, the guidelines are going to continue to be informed and interpreted in most instances by the commentary where there is commentary.  Our difference is simply the very small area where the commentary may take an interpretation that is an unreasonable  interpretation of an ambiguous guideline or even tries to override unambiguous guidelines text.  But we wouldn't think that happens very often.  On the other hand, Petitioner wants to swing the pendulum way in the other direction  and have a regime of no deference under which individual district judges are just free to interpret for themselves the advice that the Commission is trying to give them, notwithstanding what the Commission is telling them.  That would be a massive upheaval that would probably cause some kind of revision to  the guidelines that, of course, wouldn't solve all the retroactive problems with the cases that are still in the system.  And there's no  point.  It makes all the sense in the world, when the Commission is reasonably saying what the Commission is trying to say, to listen to the Commission.  And that's exactly where our Goldilocks position here lands.  Now I've kind of taken Petitioner's counsel to have essentially conceded the  point -- I'm sorry, Justice Thomas.

turns.speaker: Anthony J. Dick
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  It is emphatically the province of the judiciary to say what the law is, but the advisory sentencing guidelines are not the law. They are advisory.  As a result, when  interpreting the guidelines, the question is not what the law is but, rather, what is the non-binding advice that the Commission is offering about what type of sentence should be imposed?  On that question, the sensible approach is to defer to the Commission on the meaning of its own non -binding advice and then have courts decide for themselves, based on their own independent judgment, whether to  follow that advice in deciding what type of sentence they want to impose.  Now this type of deference doesn't pose any of the problems that you get when you defer to executive agencies on the meaning of the binding rules that they promulgate and enforce.  That creates all kinds of problems  for the separation of powers and the rule of law that this Court has cut back on in its recent decisions.  But Congress gave us two very clear indications that the Commission is different from executive agencies when it comes to deference.  First, Section 706 of the APA, which applies to executive agencies, makes very clear that courts should be the ones to resolve interpretive issues.  So anytime you have an executive agency claiming authority for deference, that is a backdrop that's going to  require a very clear statement to overcome.  Second, instead of Section 706 of the APA, which does not apply to the Sentencing  Commission at all, what we have is the text of the Sentencing Reform Act, which does authorize  the Commission not only to promulgate guidelines but also to promulgate policy statements that authoritatively interpret the guidelines.  And, Justice Gorsuch, that is the square holding of Williams, which we can talk about.  In Williams, this Court held that when a policy statement interprets a guideline, that  is an authoritative interpretation of the guideline.  And then, in Stinson, this Court  simply recognized that when the Commission uses the label of "commentary" to interpret a guideline, that falls within the same statutory authority.  And Stinson starts with Williams,  and it doesn't get to Seminole Rock until after it says that there is authority to interpret the guidelines.  So, as a result of all of that, the Commission's deference that it gets is based on express statutory text.  There's no need to  rely here on any fictional presumption of implied delegation.  This Court's cases cutting  back on that fictional presumption in Loper Bright and Kisor simply don't apply.  And the deference that the Commission enjoys rests on  express authority that is just as sturdy today as it was when Stinson was decided.  Stinson should be upheld.  There's no reason to create the chaos that would come from overruling it.  And I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Kevin Joel Page
turns.text: May it please the Court: The most workable regime is one of no deference because it eliminates all threshold tests before courts are required to calculate the guidelines.  It is -- it remains a  statutory command of what is left of Booker to calculate the guidelines.  And so the Court should simply instruct the district courts to do that without asking them to decide whether the commentary is in tension with that or, if  so, how much tension.  It is also the case that if the Court were to scour the text of the Sentencing Reform Act, it will find no provision that states that  --that commentary or policy statements ought to bind the courts in the interpretation of the guidelines.  And I do believe that  -- that if the Court finds an express delegation of interpretive authority here, it will find  them all over the place.  553(b) expressly authorizes the creation of interpretative rules.  If there is an express delegation to make that bind -- to make the commentary binding, why not those as well?  But I do want to -- to point out that I think, if the Court applies the limitations  in Kisor to the commentary in the policy statements, that will actually solve many of the concerns that have been raised here today. It will resolve the  -- one concern about disuniformity in the precedent because the -- the policy statements and the commentary will be available to resolve cases of grave ambiguity.  It will resolve the  --any concerns the Court may have about stare decisis because the Court wouldn't be doing anything in the sentencing context to move from Stinson to  Kisor that it didn't do in the agency context to go from Seminole Rock to Kisor.  And if Williams pertains, it  --and I don't think a move to Kisor would undermine Williams in any way because, if Williams pertains to the interpretation of guidelines through policy statements, then there isn't any reason that Kisor wouldn't apply to that as well. As to the concern about whether or not moving to Kisor would open the floodgates to a number of resentencings, first of all, there are only a few cases of  --of tension between commentary and -- and the text of a guideline that have actually been litigated in this case, so I don't think that we can say that  --that every defendant will have an opportunity to challenge their guideline -- that it has arisen  in 2B1.1, it has arisen in -- in this case, and it has arisen in 4B1.2, and there has been one issue about the  -- the --the issue of what a dangerous weapon is, but there has not been a floodgate of people asserting, even in a world where Kisor might be thought to apply to the guidelines, that their guideline calculations are infirm.  And we can take, I think, my friend at his word and at his analysis that -- that Kisor would limit the amount of resentencing litigation that would happen or at least the  amount of resentencings as well.  Thank you.

turns.speaker: Eric Schnapper
turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: Pleading an affirmative defense is ordinarily a precondition for invoking that defense to bar or limit a claim. Kontrick held that ordinarily, under the civil rules, a defense is lost if it's not included in an amended plain -- complaint -- in an amended defense or in the original defense. There's no reason to depart in this case from those established rules. The Eleventh Circuit's Hassan decision improperly permits a defendant to invoke an affirmative defense which it has never pled. It has several fatal flaws. First, it effectively rewrites Rules 8 and 12 to create categories of affirmative defenses that do not have to be pled, despite the fact that the plain text of those rules provide that any affirmative defense and every affirmative defense must be pled. Secondly, if a defendant has not yet included an affirmative defense in its answer and the deadline under a scheduling order for amending the answer has passed, a defendant would normally have to meet the good cause standard in Rule 16(b)(4). But, under Hassan, a defendant can -- is exempt itself from that rule simply by moving for summary judgment. Third, where a defendant has inadvertently omitted an affirmative defense, Rules 15(a)(2) and 16(b)(4) establish the standard for nonetheless raising that affirmative defense. Hassan substitutes a no-prejudice standard for that. In addition, in -- in its justifications for the Hassan rule or some version of it, the defendant has offered arguments that reach far beyond just the question of what happens with an unpled affirmative defense and raises a host of issues about the -- about the issue -- the standards that would emerge. A ruling for us would simply apply the established rules and -- and standards in Rules 15(a)(2) and 16(b)(4). It would not require the Court to become embroiled in fashioning new standards, as was aired in the previous case. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Stephen J. Petrany
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: Petitioner Younge's Title VII claim fails because, as her own testimony helped to establish, she was undisputably personal staff to an elected official. Now, to be sure, the DA's office mistakenly failed to plead this defense in its answer. But the failure to comply with the pleading rules and the consequences for that mistake are two separate issues. And nothing in the federal rules holds, not 15 or 16 or anything else, that the consequence for this type of pleading mistake is that a litigant cannot raise a legal argument at summary judgment on an undisputable record where there's no prejudice to the plaintiff because nothing would have been materially different without the mistake. To the contrary, the text, structure, background principles support a prejudice test, a strict prejudice test but a prejudice test in these circumstances. That includes Rule 61, but it also includes the numerous rules that provide specific consequences like waiver, like bars on raising arguments from 12(h) to 71.1, 72(a). And conspicuously missing here is anything like that. And that silence is especially compelling because the rules used to provide that a defendant waives all defenses and objections not included in the answer. But that was removed in 1966. Younge would reinsert that atextually into the rules. Younge essentially insists that a defendant must first amend the pleadings to raise a legal argument at summary judgment. But that's not just wrong. It misunderstands what pleadings are and what they do. They provide notice of factual issues to be worked out, discovered, investigated, and ultimately tried. But legal arguments are the province of motions. And so demanding an amendment here, where the record is already set, would be empty paper-shuffling. That's what the prejudice test got you to. We have a record. What's the right answer? I think the Court should affirm. I welcome the Court's questions.

And our point is there are at least circumstances where the federal rules themselves acknowledge there are times when you don't have to amend for amendment's sake. And we think this is the example par excellence of that circumstance. I -- I will also go on to the structural reason for this. There are pleadings which cover factual issues, and there's motions which cover legal arguments. This Court has summarily reversed lower courts for requiring law in complaints. I think that you would be really undermining that understanding of the way the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure work if you say: You can't raise this legal argument on summary judgment with a completely set record, where everything is undisputable, just because it wasn't in the pleading, just because this legal argument was not in the pleading. An affirmative defense is a combination of two things: facts and law. In this case, the Eleventh Circuit held there's nothing to dispute about the facts here and there never could be. So that means we have the record. So what is the point of amending a pleading to say, oh, we have the record? The only thing left is, is there a legal argument? And legal arguments come through motions. They don't come, generally speaking, through pleadings. So we think it makes perfect sense of not only the text but the structure of the rules that in the rare circumstances where someone has made a mistake, but it just turns out that the factual record is replete, it's done, and there's nothing else you could do to it, at that point, you just treat the factual record as the factual record, and there's no reason to demand the utterly formalistic step of go amend your pleading so that it now reflects the factual record. The rules themselves reject that in 15(b)(2). And so I don't see why the Court would essentially invent a requirement of that kind where the rules, again, don't require it. They used to, but they no longer do.

turns.speaker: Eric Schnapper
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, two quick points. First of all, again, to make clear our position, it is that in order to raise an unpled affirmative defense, the --the -- the answer has to be amended. It doesn't have to be a formal motion. The court could treat a summary judgment motion as a motion to amend. And I think -- I would have thought, if that wasn't clear from our opening brief, I'm making it clear now. The opening brief criticized the Eleventh Circuit because its standard was different than 15(a)(2) and 16(a)(4), and that's our concern. One other point. My friend noted that there are some provisions in the rules which permit a defendant to invoke an affirmative defense without pleading it and suggested that that shows that you don't need to plead it at all. Those exceptions actually show the opposite because they are validly exceptions. So the first one is: An unpled affirmative defense can be raised in a 12(b)(6) motion if the affirmative defense is apparent on the face of the complaint. That's because, in the second sentence of Rule 12(b), after saying every affirmative defense must be pled, it says: But you can raise a defense by motion. So the "but" makes it clear it's an exception to the rule. With regard to Section 15(b)(2), which my friend referred to, that expressly says that an issue tried by consent, and that would include a defense, is before the court and gets resolved even though not pled. Again, the whole point of saying that is to make clear that, ordinarily, it would have to be pled. Thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Joshua I. Hammack
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: Outraged by the disclosure of one person's video-watching history, Congress enacted the Video Privacy Protection Act. In Section (b)(1), the Act provides for civil liability when a video tape service provider knowingly discloses personally identifiable information concerning any consumer of such provider. The Act defines three of those terms. At bottom, a video tape service provider is the kind of entity that will owe obligations under the law. Personally identifiable information is the kind of information the statute protects in (b)(1)(D) and (E). And a consumer is the kind of person whose information is protected in Section (b)(1). The Act permits disclosures with a consumer's consent, and in 2013, Congress made that consent easier to obtain, online, in advance, for up to two years. Here, Paramount Global systematically discloses personally identifiable information to Facebook without obtaining consent. These are not one-off disclosures. They happen constantly, instantly, every time someone, including a consumer, watches a video on the website. Paramount has shaped its business around these disclosures. All it needed to avoid liability was its consumers' consent, something it and Facebook agree was easy to get. Paramount just didn't get it. So it asks this Court to narrow the law by imposing an audiovisual limitation on the phrase "goods or services" in the definition of "consumer." But Congress put audiovisual limitations where it wanted them, in the definitions of both "video tape service provider" and "personally identifiable information," not in the definition of "consumer." That choice is dispositive. I welcome the Court's questions.

in Section (b)(1). The Act permits disclosures with a consumer's consent, and in 2013, Congress made that consent easier to obtain, online, in advance, for up to two years. Here, Paramount Global systematically discloses personally identifiable information to Facebook without obtaining consent. These are not one-off disclosures. They happen constantly, instantly, every time someone, including a consumer, watches a video on the website. Paramount has shaped its business around these disclosures. All it needed to avoid liability was its consumers' consent, something it and Facebook agree was easy to get. Paramount just didn't get it. So it asks this Court to narrow the law by imposing an audiovisual limitation on the phrase "goods or services" in the definition of "consumer." But Congress put audiovisual limitations where it wanted them, in the definitions of both "video tape service provider" and "personally identifiable information," not in the definition of "consumer." That choice is dispositive.
I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Paul D. Clement
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: In 1988, Congress addressed a specific problem with a tailored solution, protecting the personally identifiable information of consumers of video tape service providers. For years, the statute worked as designed. Personal protection of video --information of video consumers was protected, and there was virtually no litigation under this statute. Then, however, the plaintiffs' class action bar discovered the VPPA and its statutory and punitive damages. The key to their effort to repurpose the statute is the argument, the claim, that the statute's definition of "consumer" uses the phrase "goods or services" in an unmodified way, so one can become a consumer without ever having rented, purchased, or subscribed to a video. That argument fails at the threshold because the phrase "goods or services" is not unmodified in the statute, but it takes its meaning from the immediate surrounding text. And that immediately surrounding text makes clear that the relevant goods or services are the prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials that one could rent, purchase, subscribe to, from a video tape service provider. So just as one, when referring to goods or services from a medical service provider, would not logically refer to a cup of coffee or valet parking, when one refers to goods or services from a video tape service provider, one does not logically refer to chicken sandwiches or dog bandanas. The alternative of interpreting the statute to create a veritable army of VPPA consumers without any personal information to protect unless and until years or even decades later they watch a free video has nothing to recommend it and underscores that Petitioner is misreading the statute. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice. Just a couple of points. First, I think it's really important to keep our eye on the ball that what we're looking for here in Section (b)(1) is any consumer of such provider, any consumer. So, when we -- when we have questions about, well, what about someone who purchased a dog bandana or someone who purchased a La-Z-Boy recliner or someone who purchased something or rented something years ago, our question is made simpler by the fact that (b)(1) says any consumer of such provider. So is someone who rented something a number of years ago or purchases a chicken sandwich from a provider, is that person any consumer of such provider? The answer has to be yes. That's the most natural reading. It aligns with ordinary meaning all over the statute. Second, I want to address the --the point that my friend on the other side made regarding this shift in the number of cases brought happening, you know, a decade or so ago. And that shift did not occur because plaintiffs suddenly woke up one day and discovered the Video Privacy Protection Act. It occurred because of the advent of pixel technology, this technology that all kinds of businesses started embedding in their websites that is automatically target -- tracking and disclosing all sorts of personally identifiable information about you, including the personally identifiable information specifically defined in this statute. Third, that huge liability problem, if we get through all of the various elements of the statute and land in a world where there is large liability, I won't dispute that that's a possibility, but I think it's -- it reflects necessarily the fact that this is a huge scale disclosure regime. That large liability is only possible because of the scope of the disclosures of personally identifiable information here. Fourth, I want to address the mix-or-match point that my friend on the other side made. And I would say it's entirely unsurprising that you might mix or match as between what makes you a consumer and what gives rise to PII. That's exactly why and the direct result of the fact that Congress mentioned two different relationships to two different subject matters from the same source across those two provisions. It's the inevitable consequence of that. To go to Justice Jackson's point regarding the -- the hypothetical that you were discussing with my friend on the other side, I think that exchange really shows the incredible loophole that their reading creates where they can basically structure themselves around VPPA compliance by making sure that you request or obtain video materials or services, but we've structured our business so that you never actually rent, purchase, or subscribe to them. You'll rent, purchase, and subscribe to lots of other things but not those video materials. So, suddenly, we can disclose your personally identifiable information with impunity without your consent. That, I think, should be the anomaly when you're looking at this statute. Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice.

turns.speaker: Matthew W.H. Wessler
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: ERISA's duty of prudence is inherently flexible. As a result, this Court has consistently declined to inject judicially crafted bright-line rules into a determination of whether a complaint's allegations plausibly allege imprudence. Categorical rules, as this Court put it colorfully in Dudenhoeffer, do not readily "divide the plausible sheep from the meritless goats" because they are inconsistent with the careful, context-sensitive inquiry that both ERISA and Rule 8 require. The Ninth Circuit's "meaningful benchmark requirement" is just such a rule. Under it, a court first asks whether a complaint's performance allegations on their own can plausibly demonstrate imprudence by identifying a virtually indistinguishable fund that performed better. If the complaint fails to identify that specific fund, the performance allegations are discarded, and that is true even if the complaint relies on benchmarks selected by the fiduciaries themselves or comparators identified by benchmarking experts. In the Respondents' view, this rule is consistent with the ordinary pleading framework set forth in Twombly and Iqbal. But, under that framework, courts must assess all non-conclusory allegations together in determining if a complaint plausibly states a claim. The "meaningful benchmark requirement" precludes that assessment. And the Ninth Circuit's rule isn't even necessary. Everyone agrees that, without more, a complaint merely alleging that one fund performed better than another won't survive a motion to dismiss. The ordinary pleading standards, however, are perfectly capable of weeding out a truly meritorious --meritless claim like that. Ultimately, because the meaningful benchmark rule is both out of step with Twombly and Iqbal and an unnecessary solution in search of a problem, it should be rejected. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Matthew W.H. Wessler
turns.text: Yes, but I think the question is, what is an apple and what is an orange? And that question can't be answered by defining at the outset what can count as a relevant comparator. And I can, if I can, just give you an example. So the Ninth Circuit's rule, the meaningful benchmark definition that it adopted, requires that a specific comparator be an actually existing fund that shares similar aims, similar risks, similar potential rewards, and similar asset allocations. But imagine a complaint that identifies a potentially imprudent fund and says this fund is labeled as a growth fund, but it is underperforming another fund that is labeled as a stable value fund. Under the Ninth Circuit's definition, that attempted comparison would fail because the two funds do not share similar aims. But the point of the allegation is to demonstrate that the growth fund is underperforming even a fund that isn't attempting to maximize returns. And I think what you can see is that the Ninth Circuit's definition of this "meaningful benchmark requirement," if you trace it back, what you see is that it came from a series of Eighth Circuit decisions, a trio of Eighth Circuit decisions, in which the Eighth Circuit had crafted this rule in which it said, to state a claim, plaintiffs have to identify a meaningful benchmark. But, if you look at those cases, what's going on there is very different from the kind of case you have here. In those cases, what -- what you had was plaintiffs attempting to exclusively rely on performance allegations to state a claim. There were no non-performance allegations in the case. And the Eighth Circuit said, if all you're going to do is look just at performance allegations and try to get through a motion to dismiss, you better have a pretty tight connection between the challenged fund and whatever fund you're saying did better than that fund. But, here, the complaint in this case doesn't rely exclusively on performance allegations. And I think that's really the methodological problem of the Ninth Circuit's approach that adopted this Eighth Circuit rule and ported it over into a case in which performance allegations are just a part of the overall picture. It -- it block-ported that rule, though. And so what it said was not only do you have to identify this actually existing specific fund that must share the same objectives, risks, and rewards, but also, if the complaint doesn't identify that fund, the performance allegations are out of the holistic analysis because they, on their own, don't demonstrate imprudence.

turns.speaker: Charles L. McCloud
turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: I'd like to start today by noting that much of my friend's arguments had little to do with the question presented. The question presented today is important but narrow: Can a plaintiff state a plausible claim for a breach of the duty of prudence based on a comparison of two funds that aren't meaningfully similar? And as Judge Miller's opinion explained for the Ninth Circuit below, the answer is no for multiple reasons. You can start with ERISA's text and purpose. ERISA recognizes that fiduciaries can make a wide range of prudent decisions, including the decision that Intel's fiduciaries made here to pursue a more conservative strategy through diversification. Just because one strategy produces lower returns doesn't make it imprudent. And, in assessing prudence, the statute commands a comparison to a fiduciary with like aims acting in like capacity, not an identical fiduciary and not identical investments but similar enough to make the comparison meaningful. Requiring meaningful comparisons also follows from well-established federal pleading standards. Again, underperformance standing alone is not a violation of ERISA, as my friend conceded. So the mere existence of a difference in performance between two funds doesn't plausibly suggest any wrongdoing, especially when accounting for the obvious alternative explanation that different funds are designed to perform differently. To rule out that explanation, a plaintiff needs to allege that the funds being compared had similar aims but performed better or cost less. Mr. Wessler has called this requirement of an apples-to-apples comparison an improper heightened pleading standard. That's not correct. This Court regularly draws clear lines at the pleading stage. Twombly did it for allegations of parallel conduct. Dudenhoeffer did it for allegations based on insider information. Hikma did it most recently for allegations based on inaction. The meaningful benchmark standard does the same thing for allegations that a fund costs too much or didn't earn enough. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Aimee Brown
turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: ERISA allows prudent fiduciaries to make a range of reasonable judgments when adopting investment objectives. They can pursue varying degrees of exposure to market upside and varying degrees of protection from market downside. When different objectives lead to different results, that does not suggest imprudence. In this case, Intel's fiduciaries had the objective of reducing exposure to losses at the acknowledged expense of some potential upside. Petitioners have not challenged the prudence of that objective. Instead, they have asked the lower courts to infer that the fiduciaries imprudently implemented that objective based on the fact that Intel's funds underperformed other funds. But, to create that inference, Petitioners have to compare Intel's funds to other funds with similar objectives. Otherwise, the obvious alternative explanation for the difference in results is the difference in objectives. That common-sense understanding does not mean that plaintiffs in every case need to plead a comparator. There are myriad ways of pleading imprudence without relying on performance at all. But, when a claim is premised on underperformance, the comparator has to be similar to make the comparison probative of the claim. I welcome the Court's questions.

I think the easiest way to do that is to assess it within the confines of what we're doing with the duty of prudence. Prudence is about process and not about performance. In a case like this, that's going to mean that the plaintiff is essentially alleging that if its fiduciaries were acting prudently, they would have selected the better-performing fund. But, again, in order for that to be the correct inference, you have to hold constant the things that go into that decision that the Petitioners are not challenging as imprudent themselves. But, without that kind of comparison that holds constant the factors that go into the decision, the -- the implication just isn't there. And it might be helpful to actually apply that to this case and to show how the Ninth Circuit, I think, did that correctly because, here, the plaintiffs identified funds that had different objectives entirely from Intel's objective.
