turns.speaker: Aimee Brown
turns.text: I think it's correct that the Ninth Circuit first looked at the underperformance allegations and determined whether those under -- whether those allegations were going to be probative at all in the analysis, and it held that they were not. I don't think that that's incorrect to -- to do that that way. I think that's very consistent with Twombly, for example. In order for those allegations to do any work, they have to be tied to a meaningful comparator because, otherwise, they are equally consistent with the lawful alternative explanation here that these just had different objectives, and so the different results don't tell you anything. That's not enough to take the complaint outside of neutral territory, is the term that Twombly uses at one point. But then I think the Ninth Circuit did continue on to look at all of the rest of the allegations in the complaint and assess them on their own merit to see if those allegations moved the complaint outside of neutral territory. They were insufficient on their own for reasons that had nothing to do with underperformance, as Mr. McCloud was saying. I do want to reiterate, though, that we agree that there is going to be circumstances in which it's very possible to plead these kinds of complaints without any need for underperformance allegations at all. And that can be the case when you are challenging both, you know, the overall objective that the fund is adopting, or it could be the case even when you're challenging the implementation of that objective. So, if you had a fund, for example, that stated that its objective was be --to be quite conservative and to not have a lot of exposure to market downside, and then they -they turned around and invested, you know, percent of their assets in the biotech industry alone, that on its face is just inconsistent with the --with the objective that they have announced. I don't think you need to find a comparator in order to make that kind of claim. And I think the same thing is going to be true for allegations that go to the strategy itself. You're not necessarily -- or go to the overall objective itself. You don't necessarily need a comparator. The cases in which a comparator has generally been more useful is when you're challenging fees because it can be helpful to see kind of what else is on the market fees-wise. Even in those cases, you know, if you -- if you made some kind of allegation that the -- the -- the fees you're paying are for duplicative services or something like that, that can be a situation in which you don't need a comparator too. So it really all depends on whether the Petitioner or the plaintiff in this case has decided to put that comparison in the complaint. That's when this kind of benchmark analysis is going to come into play.

turns.speaker: Matthew W.H. Wessler
turns.text: Thank you. Just a few quick points in rebuttal. You just heard the government agree that the Ninth Circuit's approach requires isolating a specific subset of allegations and asking, separate and apart from the rest of the allegations, whether those isolated allegations are sufficient to permit an inference of imprudence. That is flatly inconsistent with Rule and the approach that this Court has said time and again applies to ERISA as it does everywhere else, that all of the allegations have to be taken together and assessed holistically. I think that matters in a case like this, where you have an allegation about an imprudent either strategy or implementation of that strategy that then turns out badly. The performance allegations play a significant role in allowing a court to assess whether, taken together, they permit a plausible inference of imprudence, but that kind of holistic analysis is foreclosed under the Ninth Circuit's approach. I also would caution this Court against attempting to define at the outset what can count as meaningful in this context. It's ultimately a project doomed to fail because it doesn't take account of the broad range of contexts in which some kind of comparator could be relevant. Is it aims? Is it asset allocations? Is it risks? All of that could be relevant, or none of it could be relevant. And a -- and an attempt to provide a comparator could be pointing to a dissimilar fund that is different in the kinds of aims or objectives that the challenged fund has. That's why Rule 8 contemplates -- and ERISA as well -- a context-specific inquiry that doesn't rely on the kind of bright-line rules that the Ninth Circuit embraced here. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Nicholas R. Reaves
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: The Archdiocese of Denver schools exist to pass on the faith to the next generation. To do this, they ask all families who enroll to be open to and supportive of the church's teachings. Because of this sincere religious exercise, the State has denied Colorado families the ability to use Universal Preschool funding at Catholic schools. Under this Court's public benefits cases, that triggers strict scrutiny. The Tenth Circuit was wrong to cabin that precedent that this Court reaffirmed in Carson to explicit religious exclusions only. That can't be reconciled with Sherbert, Thomas, or Mahmoud. Nor can it be reconciled with this Court's instruction in Carson to look to the operation and the effect of the law, not for magic words. After rejecting Carson, the Tenth Circuit applied Smith, but this too was wrong. When Colorado allows over a thousand schools to turn families away for a variety of different reasons, it has created a flexible and customizable program, nothing like the generally applicable across-the-board laws that Smith envisioned. And Colorado's inconsistent and contradictory arguments further confirm the State's actions are anything but generally applicable. Colorado has flexibly interpreted the mandate to accommodate important secular interests, but it's called the same law a hard limit when Petitioners sought a religious accommodation. And Colorado has discretion via the catch-all exemption to permit preschools to organize around "specific competencies or interests" and to serve "specific communities." Yet it has refused to extend that flexible treatment to Petitioners. Finally, this is not a zero-sum game. Letting families use Universal Preschool funding at Catholic schools won't take away a single seat from the over 2,000 preschools already participating in the program. In fact, letting Catholic schools in will create more seats for everyone, even for families who disagree with Catholic teachings. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Sarah M. Harris
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: There are two main paths to reversal. First, this Court could hold that public benefits programs that condition eligibility for benefits on foregoing otherwise lawful religious exercise trigger strict scrutiny. That's the rule Carson distilled from Sherbert, and that rule makes particular sense for educational benefits given the Court's longstanding recognition that religious education is vital to many faiths. Second, this Court could hold that Colorado's pre -- pre-K benefits regime triggers strict scrutiny under any approach because it isn't generally applicable. Either way, Colorado can't satisfy strict scrutiny. The better path in our view, though, would be to go with the first course, as Petitioner has emphasized. At this point, the doctrine is at a point where the Court should decide whether Sherbert survives. Carson puts that in sharp relief. And the Court's most recent decision in Mahmoud creates an especially untenable situation in the educational context because parents have strict scrutiny in this context and yet religious schools would not in many of the same claims. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Helen Norton
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: Colorado welcomes religious preschools to UPK. The only thing Colorado asks is that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet, religious and secular alike. UPK is neutral towards religion. Well before this Court's decision in Carson, Colorado made three key choices. First, it expanded free high-quality preschool to every four-year-old in the state when, before, its predecessor program focused only on low-income and disabled children. Second, it replaced its public school-only approach with a public/private partnership that welcomes private schools, including religious schools that teach religious education. And, third, it holds all participating preschools to the same standards, including student-teacher ratios, class sizes, teacher training obligations, and equal opportunity. Under this program, faith-based preschools remain free to teach their religious beliefs, including their beliefs about sex or gender or marriage, free to teach them while receiving public funding. Under this program, publicly funded preschools choose their curriculum, and families, regardless of their protected class status, choose what schools to attend. But families have no right to change a school's curriculum. Finally, UPK's equal opportunity requirements are generally applicable. The statute requires that disabled and low-income children receive additional and specialized services because having a disability or living in poverty directly interferes with those children's ability to benefit from preschool at all. UPK does not devalue religion by allowing preschools to remove these barriers. The judgment below should be affirmed. I welcome this Court's questions.

turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice. First, a few factual points. There were a few questions about the record and the history of this case. I would first direct the Court to 306a in the Petition Appendix. That's where it talks about the fact that these Catholic schools were licensed for decades and there was not a single complaint of -- of anyone being excluded or turned away based on LGBTQ status at all. In addition, if we're talking about access to these preschools, I actually think the fifth grade example, which my friend on the other side pointed to, supports our position. The testimony at trial in that case was that this family came to the school, they met with the principal, they learned about the school's beliefs, and at the end of the day, it was a mutual decision that this was not the right fit for that family. That's the only example that's in the record. We also looked into it, and there are two UPK preschools currently in the program today within three miles of every single Catholic preschool in the Archdiocese. This is just not really a problem in real life. And -and Colorado's own expert said any harm was speculative. That's at JA 419. And in terms of, you know, what actually happened in this case, this case went to trial. This is not a -- a PI rushed up to this Court. We had a trial. Our witnesses testified to what the Catholic Church believes. Our witnesses testified, the preschool directors testified, the principal testified. So Colorado knows the facts. On JA 147, there's testimony that we submitted a -- an application. One of the Catholic preschools submitted an application to the program explaining what the religious beliefs are, and Colorado did not respond. So we've tried to participate in this program. A couple additional points. You know, when the state violates the Constitution, there might be multiple problems with what the state is doing. And I think that's what you see in Carson. In Carson, there's certainly a neutrality analysis, but I don't take that to be the only problem. And I think the first half of this Court's opinion makes that clear. In addition, Colorado cannot co-opt a religious school just because they think they provide a good education or an education that might be a good fit for certain families. That's this Court's decision in 303 Creative. In terms of the strict scrutiny analysis, I don't think you need to say anything more than you already said in Fulton. This is an even easier case than Fulton in terms of the strict scrutiny analysis. At the end of the day, I also think what Sherbert said about neutrality is right. When talking about the preference or the accommodation that was given in Sherbert, this Court didn't say it was -- this Court disclaimed the fact that it was -- the idea that it was establishing a religion. It said, instead, this is an obligation of neutrality in the face of religious differences. That's how you should think about accommodating religion. If someone is -- is -- is different, differently situated because of their religion, an accommodation is neutrality. In terms of, you know, what this case is about at the end of the day, I also think it's important to keep in mind that this is an as-applied challenge seeking to protect the religious beliefs that this Court called decent and honorable. And the people actually being excluded or being denied are families. It's -it's Dan and Lisa Sheley, who are out $18,000 because of their religious exercise. Thank you.

turns.speaker: William R. Peterson
turns.text: Thank you. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: AEDPA's restrictions on second or successive habeas applications reflect the balance struck by Congress between finality and error correction. Rather than pursue error correction at all costs, Congress chose to allow new claims in these applications only in limited circumstances that do not include changes in the diagnostic standards for intellectual disability. This Court decided Atkins versus Virginia and announced the rule that the Constitution prohibits capital punishment of the intellectually disabled before Respondent even committed his crimes. And Respondent relied on Atkins versus Virginia in his initial federal habeas application. The rule of Atkins is not a new rule of constitutional law that was previously unavailable to him under Section 2244(b)(2)(A). And Moore versus Texas, which was a legal change following Respondent's initial federal habeas application, has not been made retroactive to cases on collateral review by this Court. Nor can Respondent pass through the gateway of Section 2244(b)(2)(B) because the facts underlying his claim are unrelated to his guilt for the underlying offense. This Court should defer to Congress's policy choices, correct the Fifth Circuit's interpretation of Section 2244(b)(2)(A), and reverse. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Jeremy Schepers
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: The Fifth Circuit correctly interpreted the federal successor statute. It did so according to the ordinary meaning of that statute's words. Under that interpretation, a rule is new when the case in question announced a novel legal standard. It's retroactive when this Court has said so. And a claim relying on that rule is previously unavailable if it had no possibility of merit under the governing legal standard. In contrast, the Petitioner and the United States assert that a rule is available simply when it's been announced. But existence and availability aren't the same thing. Many things exist that aren't necessarily available to us. This Court's decisions in Booth and Ross strongly support the Fifth Circuit's rule here. There, this Court held that "available" means "capable of use" and that it requires the possibility of some relief. Importantly, in those cases, that was relief to the specific prisoner in question, not just whether the grievance system generally was capable of providing relief. Much has been discussed regarding the clinical standards of intellectual disability as being facts, and while that's certainly true in some sense, there are also facts with important legal significance. This Court has described those standards as the fundamental premise of its Atkins decision. When those standards change, the Eighth Amendment's protected class potentially changes as well. And in those rare circumstances, that can render a rule legally available for the first time, as it does here for Mr. Johnson. But those changes are, in fact, rare. Mr. Johnson is the only individual who has been authorized to proceed based off of the changes in 2013 in the DSM-5. And when the DSM was again updated in 2022, no one has been authorized to proceed under those changes. I welcome the Court's questions.

The inquiry here is what has changed from the previous federal habeas application that the prisoner has filed. There have been discussion about the extent to which the DSM is incorporated into Atkins itself. I -- I think the hypothetical would be not necessarily a narrower DSM-6 but a much broader DSM-6, a DSM-6 that said every person with an IQ under 85 is intellectually disabled. turns.speaker: Masha G. Hansford
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: Mr. Maxwell's claim in this case is that he's being held in prison in violation of federal law because the First Step Act requires his release from prison and transfer to home confinement or to a halfway house. That is a distinct and lower level of custody. That claim falls squarely within the text of the federal habeas statute because it asserts that Respondent, the Warden of Mr. Maxwell's prison, is holding him "in custody in violation of the laws of the United States." It also falls within the core historical province of the Great Writ. And it is materially indistinguishable from this Court's decision in Preiser against Rodriguez, which held that claims seeking release from prison to parole must be brought in habeas. The Fifth Circuit dismissed Mr. Maxwell's case on the ground that habeas is only available where a prisoner seeks complete release. No one defends that rule here. The government, as Respondent, agrees that habeas is the appropriate vehicle and, despite gesturing at a few supposed off-ramps, supports vacatur of the decision below. Even amicus appointed to defend the judgment below does not endeavor to defend the reasoning of the Fifth Circuit. Instead, amicus acknowledges that habeas is available for some level-of-custody claims, but he argues not for Mr. Maxwell's claim here. Amicus's efforts to limit habeas finds no footing in statutory text or in history, and he offers no principled basis for distinguishing the types of claims that are in from those that are out. Perhaps most starkly, amicus cannot distinguish FSA prerelease custody from parole given the legal and practical similarities between the two. Congress put transfer to prerelease custody for prisoners to earn good-time credits at the heart of the First Step Act. When a warden fails to release a prisoner under that authority, habeas is available. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.text: Absolutely, Justice Thomas. Happy to address both. To start with the 3621(b) argument, the government, in its brief, raised the possibility that there's a judicial review bar. But that argument -- that provision does not apply to the claims in this case. 3621(b) says not -- a designation of a place of imprisonment under this subsection is not reviewable in any court. That's a determination under 3621(b). Mr. Maxwell's claim in this case is not a challenge to anything the BOP did under 3621(b). It is an assertion under 3624(g) and 3634(d)(4) -- (d)(4)(C), which is the right to be transferred, not BOP's discretionary decision. And I think that the --the First Step Act very clearly treats that as its own distinct form of release. In particular, you can look at 3624(g)(2) and 3624(g)(4) that talk about prisoners placed in prerelease custody pursuant to this subsection as in 3624. So it is a different authority. And we're not invoking the 3621(b). Now, to the extent that the ultimate decision as to which halfway house, Halfway House A or B, still goes through 3621(b), I think that itself is not clear because I think there are regulations that are supposed to adopt the 3621(b) standards pursuant to 3624(c)(6). turns.speaker: Kevin J. Barber
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: If Petitioner has any avenue for his habeas claim -- or his First Step Act claim, habeas is the one. Under Preiser and this Court's related cases, habeas is the vehicle for a prisoner's claim alleging unlawfully prolonged confinement in prison even if the liberty he seeks is conditional. That narrow basic principle resolves this case, so there's no need to adopt Petitioner's amorphous level-of-custody rule. Amicus's approach, on the other hand, can't salvage the decision below. So, if the Court does decide the question presented despite the judicial review bar in Section 3621(b) and the impending mootness of this case, it should vacate the judgment of the court of appeals. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.speaker: Brian W. Barnes
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: Federal prisoners typically want two things: better, less restrictive conditions of confinement and earlier release from custody. If Petitioner wins this lawsuit, his term of imprisonment won't be shortened by even a single day, and he will remain subject to control by the Bureau of Prisons. Under the plain terms of this statutory regime, prerelease custody isn't release, and home confinement is a form of confinement. Petitioner isn't suing for release but for a change in the location where he will serve the remainder of his prison sentence. That places this case on the conditions of confinement side of the line and makes habeas the wrong vehicle for Petitioner's claim. The parties treat as self-evident the difference between incarceration in a prison on the one hand and a halfway house or home confinement on the other. But the reality of the federal prison system isn't so simple. A federal prisoner moving from a prison camp to a halfway house may be moving from one facility with dormitory-style housing and no perimeter fence that he leaves to work off site to another facility with all those same attributes. A move between two such facilities is not the sort of quantum change in the level of custody that Preiser and its progeny place at the core of habeas corpus. For that reason, Petitioner's claim to entitlement to credits under the First Step Act may be pursued, if at all, only as a civil rights claim. The Court should affirm the Fifth Circuit's judgment. And I welcome the Court's questions.
